## Spatial areas available in pacea, and how to create your own

We have some spatial areas saved in
pacea, technically as sf (spatial features) polygon or
multipolygon data objects. We hope to include many fisheries management areas soon, as being
discussed in our [GitHub Issue](https://github.com/pbs-assess/pacea/issues/8). 

We first show how these can be used, and then show how to create your own custom
areas using our helper functions.

## Current areas

The current areas are:

```{r, which_areas, echo = FALSE}
areas_in_pacea <- which_data_are_areas()
```

```{r, areas_table, echo = FALSE}
# Create table
areas_table <- tibble::tibble(
  `Area name` = areas_in_pacea,
  Description = sapply(areas_in_pacea, 
                       get_rd_title)
)

knitr::kable(areas_table)
```

(Developers - see the hidden code here to check for new areas).
```{r, plot_areas, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 6, echo = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# Look at these manually to check they are actually areas. 
# For any new ones that are not, just add them to the `ignore` 
#  default in which_data_are_areas().

for(area_name in areas_in_pacea) {
  area_data <- get(area_name)
  plot(area_data,
       main = area_name)
}
```

## Using areas

We can easily restrict spatial data within our plotting functions, or
using `restrict_to_area()` for doing analyses. 

We
will first use the Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST)
data described in the 
[OISST vignette](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/oisst.html), 

To just restrict a plot to an area, as an example we use the elusive pacea area
called `sasquatch` and then plot each March to September from 2014 to 2016:
```{r, areaplots}
plot(oisst_month,
     months = 3:9,
     years = 2014:2016,
     area = sasquatch)
```
We can add options to restrict the plot to the reduced area, and to add an
outline (the default is the last month of data):
```{r, areaplots2}
plot(oisst_month,
     area = sasquatch,
     restrict_plot = TRUE,
     area_outline = sasquatch)
```
This apparently whimsical plot is instructive in showing that the restriction to
the area for `oisst_month` is based on whether the centre of each cell is
within the sasquatch or not. The geometry of the `oisst_month` data is POINT
(in sf speak), not polygons, to save filesize:
```{r, oisstgeom}
sf::st_geometry(oisst_month)
```

We can similarly restrict the area of plotting of the BCCM output (the first
line either downloads the output or loads it into R; see the BCCM vignette):
```{r, sasquatchprimaryproduction}
primary_production <- bccm_primaryproduction_full()   

plot(primary_production, 
     area = sasquatch,
     restrict_plot = FALSE,
     area_outline = sasquatch)
```

Looking more closely, we can see that, unlike the `oisst_month` eample above,
any cells that are at all inside the area are included:
```{r, sasquatchprimaryproduction2}
plot(primary_production, 
     area = sasquatch,
     restrict_plot = TRUE,
     area_outline = sasquatch)
```
This is because the geometry of the BCCM results are POLYGONS:
```{r, bccmgeom}
sf::st_geometry(primary_production)
```
Internally, `plot.pacea_st()`, which the `plot()` calls above are using, is
using `sf::st_intersects()` to calculate intersection locations between the main
data set (e.g. `primary_production`) and the `area`. The `sf::st_intersects()`
function returns `TRUE` when features intersect, or even just touch. 

For the `oisst_month` example that uses points as the centre of grid cells, the cell
is included in the plot (i.e. is within the area) if the point representing it
is within the area. Hence, if the point is outside the area (even if some of the
grid cell is within it), then the cell is excluded and we see the white areas
inside the sasquatch area.

But for the BCCM `primary_production` values, the geometry is polygons, and so
if any part of a grid cell (represented by a polygon) touches the area then that
cell is included. Hence there is no white within the area in this case. Note the
differing resolution of the underlying grid cells between the two examples (but
this is not relevant here).

If necessary, you can create your own area (as an sf object) from a matrix or tibble of latitude
and longitude values, using our `create_area_sf_polygon()` function (if the
first and last rows are different then the function repeats the first row as the
last to make an enclosed polygon). Using a matrix or tibble gives the same result:
```{r, myarea}
my_area_matrix <- matrix(c(-130, -132, -130, -128,
                           48, 50, 52, 50),
                         ncol = 2)
my_area_matrix
my_area_1 <- create_area_sf_polygon(my_area_matrix)
my_area_1

my_area_tibble <- tibble::tibble(
  lon = c(-130, -132, -130, -128),
  lat = c(48, 50, 52, 50))
my_area_tibble
my_area_2 <- create_area_sf_polygon(my_area_tibble)
expect_equal(my_area_1,
             my_area_2)
```

Quick example to check that the normalised index of mean anomalies is same
as normalised index of mean of means. Think so since both relative to the same
climatology. TODO. Also it's still based on climatology; so does mean of actual
values just give the same? 

```{r, buoysst}
sst_west_dixon_apr_using_anomalies <- create_index(buoy_sst)
sst_west_dixon_apr_using_mean <- create_index(buoy_sst, buoy_statistic = "mean")
expect_equal(sst_west_dixon_apr_using_anomalies,
             sst_west_dixon_apr_using_mean)
# Not convinced that will always hold though, I think only difference would be
# if you did not have a climatology for a particular month, which does not
# happen with the default years. So probably best to keep the generality.
```
